Abstract\\nIn efforts to predict the long-distance travel impacts  (for passengers and freight)  of self-driving cars and trucks\\nacross Texas and the US,  researchers estimated models for long-distance domestic passenger and freight trips\\nbefore and after the introduction of autonomous vehicles (AVs)  and applied the passenger models to a 10%\\nsynthetic US  population (12.1M  households and  28.1M  individuals across 73,056  census tracts). To generate\\ndisaggregated passenger trips,  travel demand models—including trip frequency, season, purpose, party size,\\nmode choice,  and  destination choice models—and a vehicle ownership model were estimated. Different\\ndatasets,  including a 2021 long-  distance passenger AV  survey designed in this study, the 2016/17 National\\nHousehold  Travel  Survey, and EPA Smart  Location and FHWA  rJourney datasets,  were used for model\\nestimation. Assuming a $3,500 technology cost  premium (e.g.,  in year 2040),  total person-miles traveled  per\\ncapita for existing long-distance trips are estimated to rise 35% (from 280 to 379 miles per month).\\nFor freight-travel impacts, a four-step  travel  demand  modeling  process was used  for trip  generation and\\ndistribution, mode choice, and traffic assignment across human-  driven trucks,  automated trucks (ATrucks),\\nrail,  and intermodal rail. When ATruck  shipping  costs  drop to half  that  of human-  driven trucks,  truck mode\\nshare is predicted  to  increase by  4.2%  (from  57.0% to 61.2%), with a 6.0% increase in ton-  miles transported  by\\ntruck. Such cost reductions are expected to increase Texas trucks’ mode splits by  over 10% on commodities\\nlike food, paper, and primary metal.\\n17.  Key Words  18. Mode share change (in ton-miles) by trip distance if ATruck cost drops\\nfrom 1.5 times HTruck cost to the same as HTruck cost .................................... 129\\n\\nxiv\\n\\n## [PDF page 16]\\n\\nExecutive Summar  y\\n\\nAs fully automated or “autonomous” vehicles (AVs) become increasingly\\navailable in the coming years, their travel, trade, emissions, cost, and other\\nimplications need to be anticipated. Prior studies predict AVs dominating US\\npassenger travel between 100 and 500 miles (one-way) and freight travel of over\\n300 ton-miles. With network vehicle-miles traveled (VMT) predicted to rise by\\nover 25% (due to many Texas air travelers shifting to shared AVs, others\\nextending their current ground-trip distances, and still others making more trips),\\nthis project gathered new data to simulate changes in freight and passenger flows\\nacross Texas and the US for all competing modes in the future. Integrating related\\ntrends like AV technology price change, the research team anticipated the impacts\\nof AVs on passenger mode and destination choice for long-distance trips over 75\\nmiles as well as the impacts of automated trucks (ATrucks) on freight travel.\\n\\nThe team designed and distributed a long-distance passenger-travel survey with\\nalmost 70 questions (as described in Chapter 2, Chapter 3, and Appendix A)\\ntackling aspects of long-distance travel, AVs, and shared autonomous vehicle\\n(SAV) use, as well as the COVID-19 pandemic’s effects on long-distance travel.\\nThe survey included  a mix of revealed and stated preference questions for\\nreasonably  recent long-distance trips and future scenarios. The survey responses\\nfrom 1,004 individuals (45% Texans and 55% other US residents) indicated that\\nTexans were about 40% more willing to travel long-distance using AVs than other\\nUS respondents in scenarios where the use of AVs imposes a 0–50% increase in\\ntravel time. Texans reacted similarly to other US respondents in scenarios where\\nlong-distance AV trips impose an added cost (60% were “unlikely” to travel in an\\nAV that incurred a 50% cost increase, and 37% were “unlikely” to choose an AV\\nwhen it would increase costs by 25%). More than 40% of Texans were\\n“absolutely” or “more likely” to use AVs for a long-distance trip than before the\\npandemic if it didn’t impact costs. If AV travel decreased long-distance travel\\ncosts by half, the share of Texans who would be at least “more likely” to travel in\\nan AV went up to almost 60%. For 60% of Texans, using an AV would not\\nchange their destination choice, but about 20% would decide to visit a place that’s\\nfarther away. Regarding increasing travel party size, 32% of Texans would do so\\non a long-distance AV trip, while only 22% of others surveyed would. People\\nwho would prefer an AV for long-distance travel most related this choice to added\\nsafety, followed by reliability. Safety was also the priority for respondents who\\nopted not to use AVs for long-distance travel, and they tended to consider faulty\\nsoftware to be a potential issue. Literature Synthesis\\n\\nBefore the 1995 American Travel Survey (ATS) data (for trips over 100 miles\\none-way) became available, travel demand researchers focused mostly on urban\\nmobility and local congestion issues (Aultman-Hall, 2018). Due to rising need\\nand interest, several long-distance (or inter-city) travel surveys emerged in the\\nUS, including questions in the 2001, 2009, and 2016/17 National Household\\nTravel Surveys (NHTS) and state-focused long-distance surveys in Ohio,\\nMichigan, California, Colorado, Utah, Vermont, and Alabama. The FHWA’s\\n(2015) rJourney long-distance travel demand model incorporated data from the\\n1995 ATS, the 2001 NHTS, and long-distances surveys in California, Colorado,\\nand Ohio. European survey projects include Axhausen and Youssefzadeh’s (1999)\\nMethods for European Surveys of Travel Behaviour (MEST), Frei et al.’s (2010)\\nKnowledge-base for Intermodal Passenger Travel in Europe” (KITE), and\\nZumkeller et al.’s (2010) Intermodal Linking of Passenger Transport Modes\\nConsidering User Needs (INVERMO) project.\\n\\nLong-distance trips are a key component of the nation’s traffic volumes,\\ncongestion levels, emissions, crashes, and pavement damage. Long-distance trips\\nare usually defined as one-way trips over 50 miles, but that definition does vary\\nby context, ranging from 75-mile (as in this report) to 100-mile trips, and out-of-\\ntown travel or overnight travel (Aultman-Hall et al., 2018; LaMondia et al.,\\n2016a; Bacon and LaMondia, 2016). According to 2016/17 NHTS trip records,\\n43.3% of US person-miles traveled (PMT) come from one-day one-way trips over\\n50 miles. These are just 2.5% of all person trips being made in the US but almost\\nhalf of all PMT (McGuckin, 2018). Although the 2001 NHTS was the last\\nnational travel survey in the US to ask about long-distance trips in detail (Hu and\\nReuscher, 2004), the 2016/17 NHTS (which focused on one-way travel during\\none survey day) estimates over 1,500 trillion miles of long-distance PMT annually\\n(McGuckin, 2018).\\n\\n1.1. Literature  Review\\nThis section reviews various aspects of the literature related to long-distance\\ntravel, including the factors impacting long-distance trip-making, new predictions\\nof inter-  and intra-regional travel patterns due to autonomous vehicles (AVs)  and\\nfully autonomous trucks  (ATrucks)  with environmental implications, long-\\ndistance tourism, and long-distance travel predictions during the COVID-19\\npandemic.\\n\\n5\\n\\n## [PDF page 21]\\n\\n1.1.1. Long-  Distance  Travel  Factors\\nGiven the distances and costs involved, long-distance travel decisions are heavily\\ninfluenced by travel cost and time considerations, and can include choices of\\nwhether and where to stay overnight en route. Long-distance personal travel is\\nmore often as compared to daily trip-making (e.g., for school, work, medical\\nappointments, and shopping). And long-distance passenger-vehicle trips tend to\\ninvolve higher occupancies than intra-urban trips (over 2 persons per long-\\ndistance trip, rather than just 1.1 for work trips and 1.3 for other intra-urban trips).\\nSchedule coordination (between members of the same travel party) is also\\nimportant, and larger vehicles tend to be used compared to those used for intra-\\nurban trip-making (LaMondia et al., 2016b).\\n\\nKey variables impacting long-distance passenger trips include frequency,\\ndistance, mode, destination, household income, traveler age, education level,\\npresence of children in the household, and more (Van Wee et al., 2006; Sandow\\nand Westin, 2010; Collia et al., 2003; Holz-Rau et al., 2014; LaMondia et al.,\\n2016a; Cho, 2013). Specific events and objectives—like professional conferences,\\nvacations, weddings, funerals, sports tournaments, and music concerts (Yang et\\nal., 2016; Burke and Woolcock, 2013; McKercher et al., 2008; Aguilera, 2008)—\\nregularly motivate long-distance travel for many different types of people.\\n\\nA key factor impacting long-distance business trip choices is employer\\nreimbursement (Schaeffer, 2009; Cai et al., 2011). For those receiving\\nreimbursement, higher-speed modes (like air travel with a ride from a\\ntransportation network company at either end) may still capture a high portion of\\nmode share in many markets, especially for business trips over 750 miles (one-\\nway). Frequent long-distance business travelers tend to be highly educated, with\\nhigher income, status, and position in their organization (Gustafson, 2012), so\\ntheir mode choices may be less affected by cost. Travel time, seat-scheduling\\nflexibility, and other factors may take center stage for that subset of long-distance\\ntravelers (Unger et al., 2016). Tourism and business purposes are key designations\\nfor long-distance passenger travel, with tourism and leisure trips happening more\\noften during holiday periods (Große et al., 2019).\\n\\nStatewide and nationwide trip models have sought to evaluate the impacts of\\nlong-distance travel (Erhardt et al., 2007; Rohr et al., 2013; Bernardin et al., 2017;\\nLaMondia et al., 2016b; Perrine et al., 2020). To anticipate congestion impacts,\\nunderstanding long-distance-trip timing is very important, with many travelers\\n(and freight carriers) purposefully avoiding the a.m. and p.m. peaks around and\\nthrough urban areas. This has been examined in some depth in past studies\\n\\n6\\n\\n## [PDF page 22]\\n\\n(Aultman-Hall et al., 2015; Sullivan et al., 2016; Scheiner, 2010; Reichert and\\nHolz-Rau, 2015).\\n\\nLi et al. (2022) conducted a 73-question online survey (with a focus on the Austin\\narea) in 2019 that captured 2,327 long-distance trips (over 100 miles each way)\\nmade by 929 respondents over the prior 12 months. Predictive models for long-\\ndistance business trips per adult per year, numbers of overnights, travel times, and\\nother travel attributes were developed; the results show that those with higher\\neducation tend to travel more often—for both business and non-business\\npurposes—everything else constant. Older and/or lower-income people are likely\\nto spend more nights at business trip destinations, as well as locations that are\\nfarther away from their origins. Persons who travel long-distance more frequently\\nare more likely to spend less time in transit or en-route, and those who travel more\\noften for business tend to spend more nights away, especially if the destination is\\nmore than 300 miles from their home.\\n\\n1.1.2. Long-  Distance  Trips  by  AVs\\nThe short-  and long-distance travel impacts of AVs have been studied in recent\\nyears, including predictions of increased national vehicle miles traveled (VMT)\\nby heavy trucks and passenger vehicles. Trip generation increase is an interesting\\nplace to start, since 19% of Americans with disabilities leave their homes\\ninfrequently and are unlikely to take long-distance trips (BTS, 2003). Harper et al.\\n(2016) estimated a 14% increase in US VMT due to travel by currently non-\\ndriving, travel-restricted, and elderly Americans thanks to AVs. Meyer and Deix\\n(2014) noted that if AVs allow disabled persons to make the same length and\\nnumber of car trips as non-disabled Americans, their VMT will rise by over 50%.\\nLee and Kockelman’s (2019) holistic look at all vectors of added passenger travel\\npredicts a 25% rise in VMT as a result of AV introduction, and Huang et al.’s\\n(2019) look at the Texas Triangle predicts a rise of over 40% in VMT for that\\nmegaregion long-term (i.e., by year 2045) due to AVs, with the number of links\\nexceeding daily capacity more than doubling.\\n\\nAVs reduce the burden of travel for drivers and may improve the quality of travel\\nfor passengers, who can now focus on more meaningful interactions with those\\npreviously focused on driving. Business travelers will be freed to work en-route to\\ntheir destination, as they would on a plane, but with no airport access, egress, or\\nwait times. Families and friends traveling together may be able to have quality\\ninteraction time while traveling with great flexibility in departure time and at a\\nreduced cost, as compared to trains and airlines. Thanks to easier “driving,” a\\ndriver’s value of travel time (VOTT), or his/her willingness to pay (WTP) to save\\ntravel time, is expected to fall 20–50% or more. LaMondia et al. (2016a) explored\\n\\n7\\n\\n## [PDF page 23]\\n\\nlong-distance mode choices originating in Michigan and forecasted that over 25%\\nof airline trips under 500 miles will shift to AVs. Such changes will have\\nimportant impacts on airlines, infrastructure planning and future land use\\n(especially on and around long-distance-transportation facilities), highway\\ncongestion, and the travel industry more generally. Gurumurthy and Kockelman\\n(2020) designed, disseminated, and then analyzed a nationwide survey on AVs’\\nimpacts on Americans’ passenger travel choices and found that AV-sharing and\\ndynamic ride-sharing should rise over time, for a variety of reasons, with shared\\nAVs (SAVs) particularly popular for long-distance business travel.\\n\\nTo analyze the impacts of AVs in the United States, Perrine et al. (2020) added a\\nnew AV mode to a subset of the rJourney mode and destination choice models.\\nWith a base scenario assuming AV operating costs to be 20% higher than those of\\nconventional vehicles, AVs reduced US airline revenues from domestic travel by\\na dramatic 53%. Availability of SAVs and AVs also shifted destination choices,\\nfor an overall 6.7% decline in US PMT from existing long-distance trip-\\ngeneration rates. Such research needs much further development and can be\\nsupplemented with newer Texas-  and long-distance-focused surveys,\\nincorporating more complete details on Texas airport offerings, airline responses,\\nand a thoughtful prediction of market shares over time (rather than simply a\\n“before” vs. long-term “after” scenario comparison). Kim et al. (2020) surveyed\\nmore than 3,000 Georgians regarding their expectations of  16 potential changes\\nbrought by AVs. Results show that more than half of the respondents expressed\\nenthusiasm for changing their activity patterns due to AVs, in terms of conducting\\nmore leisure and long-distance travel, as well as traveling to farther destinations.\\n\\n1.1.3. Automated  Trucking\\nMost existing AV studies focus on intra-urban trip-making, but few (Huang et al.,\\n2019, Huang and Kockelman, 2019) anticipate changes in freight transport. Fully\\nautomated, self  -driving trucks or “ATrucks” are those that can leave truck\\nterminals and travel to a destination without human intervention (Viscelli, 2018).\\nATrucks may be equipped with other automated functions, like drop-offs and\\npick-ups, but most experts expect an attendant on board, doing other types of\\nwork, sleeping as needed, and ensuring successful deliveries and pickups while\\nprotecting the truck asset and its cargo en route (Yankelevich, et al., 2018).\\nVehicle attendants’ ability to multi-task  will allow for extended use of\\ncommercial trucks (e.g., every day, closer to 24 hours a day) and greater labor\\nproductivity, resulting in lower per-mile and per-ton-mile freight delivery costs.\\n\\nTrucks carry over 2 trillion ton-miles of freight around the US each year, which is\\nalmost 40% of the nation’s total (BTS, 2017). Investment in and use of ATrucks\\n\\n8\\n\\n## [PDF page 24]\\n\\nwill affect not only national and regional economies (Clements and Kockelman,\\n2017) but trade patterns, production levels, and goods pricing. Commercial trucks\\nconsume about 20% of the nation’s transportation fuel, and self-driving\\ntechnologies are predicted to reduce those diesel fuel bills by 4 to 7% (Barth et\\nal., 2004; Shladover et al., 2006).\\n\\nATrucks can reduce some environmental impacts, lower crash rates, and increase\\nefficiency in warehousing operations, line-haul transportation, and last-mile\\ndeliveries. Platooned convoys should enable following truck drivers to avoid\\ncertain restrictions on service hours, enabling longer driving distances. Uranga\\n(2017) predicts greater use of ATrucks before passenger vehicle automation,\\nthanks to the more obvious economic benefits of self-driving trucks (which start\\nwith higher price tags as investment is less of a cost burden for trucking\\ncompanies relative to personal travelers).\\n\\nHuang and Kockelman (2019) anticipated changes in US highway and rail trade\\npatterns in the long-term, following widespread ATruck availability. They used a\\nrandom-utility-based multiregional input-output (RUBMRIO) model, driven by\\nforeign export demands, to simulate changes in freight flows among 3,109 US\\ncounties and 117 export zones via a nested-logit model for shipment or input\\norigin and mode, including the shipper’s choice between ATrucks and\\nconventional or human-driven trucks (HTrucks). Mode and shipment-origin\\nchoices (by freight carrier) were investigated to see how freight flow patterns\\nwould shift based on cost and operations changes due to vehicle automation. An\\nATruck’s total ownership and operation cost (normalized per mile of driving) was\\nassumed to be 25% lower than that of a conventional truck, thanks to some safety\\nbenefits (per mile traveled), fewer rest stops (thus more productive use of the\\nvehicle and the operator, if one is on board, who can stay with the expensive\\nvehicle and help with pickups and deliveries), and much better use of the on-\\nboard operator, who can do work that adds value while en route (e.g., taking the\\nplace of office staff, thereby reducing the shipping firm’s payroll). Such savings\\nhelp offset the higher acquisition cost of a self-driving truck (relative to a\\nconventional heavy-duty truck).\\n\\nDifferent VOTT and cost scenarios were explored, to provide a sense of variation\\nin the uncertain future of ground-based trade flows. Using the current US Freight\\nAnalysis Framework (FAF) data for travel times and costs—and assuming that\\nATrucks lower trucking costs by 25% (per ton-mile delivered)—truck flow values\\nin ton-miles were predicted to rise 11% due to automation’s lowering of trucking\\ncosts, while rail flow values fall 4.8%. Rail flows were predicted to rise 6.6% for\\ntrip distances between 1,000 and 1,500 miles, with truck volumes rising for all\\nother distance bands. All major cities were predicted to see lower rail flows\\n9\\n\\n## [PDF page 25]\\n\\n(inbound and outbound), with San Jose, CA, and Washington, DC, experiencing\\nmore than 70% reductions in outbound rail flows. Truck flows were also\\npredicted to lose many interactions between the northwestern US and Florida and\\nnortheastern states, while experiencing greater interactions along the western US\\n(between California and Oregon), and also between the Great Lakes region\\n(including Michigan and Illinois) and California. Rail flows were estimated to rise\\nonly in and around New Mexico, while dropping noticeably elsewhere (e.g., in\\nTexas and from San Francisco and Arizona to the Great Lakes and northeastern\\nareas, respectively).\\n\\n1.1.4. AVs’  Effects on  Intra-  Regional  Travel  Patterns\\nTo date, there have been more than 20 simulations of AVs’ and SAVs’ effects on\\nwithin-region travel. For example, Childress et al. (2015) used a Seattle,\\nWashington, activity-based travel model (including short-term travel choices and\\nlong-term work-location and auto-ownership choices) to anticipate AVs’ impacts\\non regional travel (assuming higher roadway capacities, lowered VOTT, reduced\\nparking costs, and increased car-sharing). They estimated that higher-income\\nhouseholds are more likely to choose the AV mode, as costly technology and\\nVOTT reductions for higher-VOTT travelers are likely to be more significant.\\nWhen SAVs cost $1.65 per mile (almost the same as current ride-sharing taxi\\nservices, like Lyft and Uber), drive-alone trips were estimated to fall by one-third\\nand transit shares  to rise by 140%, since modeled households let go of\\nconventional vehicles and bought AVs, or shifted to SAVs as well as other travel\\noptions.\\n\\nZhao and Kockelman (2018) extended Capital Area Metropolitan Planning\\nOrganization’s  (CAMPO)  demand model for the Austin region to include AV and\\nSAV mode options and predicted a 20% rise in regional VMT over a 10-year\\nhorizon, assuming AVs and SAVs were widely available. Without shorter\\nheadways and common use of ride-sharing (between strangers), congestion would\\nworsen. Liu et al. (2017) simulated conventional vehicles and SAVs in the Austin\\nnetwork using different SAV fare assumptions (e.g., $2, $1, and $0.50 per mile)\\nwith agent-based MATSim software. Assuming that the average SAV can serve\\n17 to 20 person trips per day, higher SAV fleet sizes deliver greater vehicle\\nreplacement rates, with  one SAV replacing 5.6 to 7.7 conventionally owned and\\noperated household vehicles. Martinez and Crist (2015) replaced Lisbon,\\nPortugal’s buses and cars with mid-size and small SAVs and estimated a 1:10\\nreplacement rate, along with a 6% increase in VMT. Importantly, reduced parking\\nneeds freed up sizable land areas throughout the region.\\n\\n10\\n\\n## [PDF page 26]\\n\\n1.1.5. Environmental  Implications\\nTransportation accounted for 28.5% of US greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in\\n2016, among which 41.6% was from passenger cars, 22.9% from freight trucks,\\n9% from air travel, and 2% from rail (EPA, 2018). Van Goeverden et al. (2016)\\nestimated that trips longer than 100 km (62 miles) account for 45% of VMT and\\n50% of GHG emissions due to person travel in Holland using 2011 data, and\\npassenger rail had one-third the emissions per passenger-km compared to\\nautomobile for personal trips. The Federal Aviation Administration (2015)\\nreported that relative to air travel, transit buses are less efficient in fuel\\nconsumption per passenger mile due to lower passenger vehicle occupancy, and\\nUS rail travel energy efficiency was only slightly higher.\\n\\nWhile more driving generally means more emissions from the transport sector,\\npassenger AVs are expected to be highly or fully electric, due to all the computing\\nand sensor demands on board. Wadud et al. (2016) sought to combine\\nautomation’s effects on VMT and GHG emissions but found striking variability in\\nfuture-year outcomes, since AVs can generate so much new travel, electrification\\nof vehicle drivetrains is not guaranteed, and changing power-grid feedstocks\\ndeliver very different emissions impacts. Fagnant and Kockelman (2014) micro-\\nsimulated right-sized SAV fleet operations for a 10-mile-squared “town” and\\ncompared net emissions to those from the standard US household vehicle mix.\\nThey estimated that SAV systems may raise VMT 10% or more but save a great\\ndeal of carbon monoxide and VOCs, thanks to keeping engines warm and\\ncatalytic converters hot (with very few “cold starts” for a hard-working SAV\\nfleet). When they added dynamic ride-sharing (between strangers), they were able\\nto get total VMT to fall, rather than rise (Fagnant et al., 2015). Lee and\\nKockelman’s (2019) recent work that randomizes all the possible contributions to\\nVMT and energy use suggests that the overall trend is downward on energy and\\nGHGs, thanks to most AVs being electric. But the VMT and congestion effects\\nremain stark, and in the wrong direction. Even once the US DOT and/or state\\nDOTs mandate one-second headways on highways (and eventually local streets),\\ncongestion associated with at-grade intersections and excessive VMT increases\\nwill still delay travelers.\\n\\n1.1.6. Long-  Distance  Tourism\\nDistance plays an important role in tourists’ travel behaviors, and the relationships\\nbetween distance and tourist behavior have been extensively explored. It is\\nbelieved that distance negatively affects tourists’ destination choices and tourists\\nare more likely to take short-distance rather than long-distance trips (Lee et al.,\\n2014). However, tourists’ preference for short-haul trips relates to many other\\n\\n11\\n\\n## [PDF page 27]\\n\\nfactors as well, such as time cost, financial cost, and safety concerns (McKercher,\\n2008; Xue and Zhang, 2020).\\n\\nTravel distance is commonly used to divide tourists into two groups: short-\\ndistance (short-haul) and long-distance (long-haul), since tourist behaviors change\\nabruptly once long-distance travel is established as an objective (Bao and\\nMcKercher, 2008). The definition of long-distance tourism is not decisive, and\\nmany scholars use different versions. For example, Boerjan (1995) considered\\nlong-haul travel by airplane as trips with a travel duration of more than 5 hours or\\ntravel distance of more than 3,000 miles to destination. Lehto et al. (2002) defined\\nlong-haul travel as “travel more than four nights or more by plane outside of the\\ninternational area.” As tourists’ preferences and the technologies facilitating travel\\nchange, the definition of long-haul travel is also changing.\\n\\nMany studies have been conducted to compare tourist behaviors between long-\\ndistance and short-distance travel, in terms of motivation, preferred activities,\\nlength of stay, travel intensity, and consumption. Long-distance travelers tend to\\nengage in multi-destination travel and attempt to satisfy multiple trip purposes\\n(McKercher and Cros, 2003; Tideswell and Faulkner, 1999). The long-distance\\ntraveler has a higher length of stay and travel expenditure (Jackman et al., 2020;\\nNicolau et al., 2018). Also, long-distance travelers care more about quality and\\nproduct features and tend to spend more on travel (Boerjan, 1995; Lo and Lam,\\n2004).\\n\\n1.2. 2016/17 NHTS  Long-  Distance  Data  Summary\\nThe 2016/17 NHTS data were collected with travel dates starting on April 19,\\n2016, and ending on April 25, 2017 (FHWA, 2017). A respondent’s designated\\n24-hour travel day started at 4:00 a.m. (local time) of the assigned travel day and\\nended at 3:59 a.m. of the following day. Weights were utilized to produce well-\\nbalanced population-level estimates, including weights of household, trip, person,\\nand vehicle (FHWA, 2017). Below are some explorations of the 2016/17 NHTS\\ndata, and comparisons of travel behaviors between the respondents from entire US\\nand the state of Texas. For most of the analysis, results are shown from both the\\nUS and Texas, as well as for three types of trips: trips across all distances (all-\\ndistance trips), long-distance trips greater than 50 miles one-way (LD50+ trips),\\nand long-distance trips greater than 100 miles one-way (LD100+ trips).\\n\\n1.2.1. Long-  Distance  Trips  vs.  All  Trips\\nThe differences between long-distance trips and all-distance trips are compared in\\nthis section. Figure 1  shows the percentage of person trips taken each day of the\\n\\n12\\n\\n## [PDF page 28]\\n\\nweek. The US and Texas show a similar pattern. As expected, for trips across all\\ndistances, each day of the week has similar person trips, but they are slightly more\\nlikely on weekdays. Long-distance trips (LD50+ trips and LD100+ trips) are more\\nlikely to occur on weekend days.\\n\\nFigure  1. Percentage  of one-  way  person  trips  by  day of  the week  in  both  the US (left)\\nand Texas (right)\\n\\nThe all-distance and long-distance person-trip counts by different trip purposes\\nare presented by day of the week in Figure 2 and Figure 3). Since the LD50+ and\\nLD100+ trips have a similar pattern, the figures compare only the all-distance\\ntrips and LD50+ trips. COVID-19’s Effects on  US  Households and\\nPassenger Travel\\nThe COVID-19 pandemic has impacted the transportation system and travel\\nbehaviors, especially long-distance travel. Almost all modes and all purposes of\\ntrips witnessed a worldwide drop from February to May 2020 (Beck and Hensher,\\n2020;  Molloy et al., 2020). More people tend to work from home during the\\npandemic (Wang, 2020; Geman, 2020), and telecommuting is expected to\\ncontinue long after the pandemic, based on a survey during late March 2020,\\nwhen half of the employed adult respondents were working from home (Guyot\\nand Sawhill, 2020).\\n\\n1.3.1. Travel Trends During COVID  -19\\nSince people hesitate to use shared modes during COVID-19, public transit has\\nbeen extensively affected (Beck and Hensher, 2020; Transit, 2020; Wang et al.,\\n2020). According to the Bureau of Transportation Statistics (2020), there was a\\n30–50% reduction in trips less than 25 miles between March and September 2020\\nin the US, compared to 2019. Trips between 25 and 100 miles  dropped at the\\nbeginning of March and reached their lowest point in early April, a roughly 47%\\nreduction compared to the same time in 2019, but the trend began to recover and\\nremained stable (about 20% reduction vs. 2019) after May. Interestingly,\\ncompared to a stable trend in 2019, trips longer than 100 miles in 2020 first\\nwitnessed a small peak pre-pandemic but dropped to their lowest point, about a\\n30% reduction, in April. Then, however, the trend began to bounce back to\\nnormal, reaching 2019 levels at the end of May, and exceeding them by 64% at\\nthe end of August 2019. The same reduction trend was witnessed for US\\ncommercial flights, both domestic and international, which experienced a nearly\\n70% drop in mid-April, but then domestic flights started to revive  from their\\nearlier drops with a slight increase seen for international flights. International\\npassenger vehicle trips, which presumably are long-distance trips, also greatly\\ndecreased during the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic.\\n\\n22\\n\\n## [PDF page 38]\\n\\nA similar trend of trip counts and mode share has been observed in many other\\ncountries. In Switzerland, there was widespread suppression of travel demand\\nacross almost all modes during the pandemic (Molloy et al., 2020). In Australia,\\ncommuting trips fell from an average of seven per week down to three, and half of\\nrespondents canceled their planned air travel (Beck and Hensher, 2020). In India,\\nabout 41% of commuters stopped traveling during the transition to the lockdown\\nphase, and 5.3% of commuters shifted from public to private modes (Pawar,\\n2020). However, biking has become more popular during the pandemic, with trips\\nincreasing by 22% in places such as Greater Manchester in the UK (Rannard,\\n2020), inducing some short-distance trips. The same trend has been observed in\\nSwitzerland (Molloy et al., 2020), where biking trip lengths increased up to a\\n180% in early April.\\n\\nOverall, COVID-19 has disrupted long-distance travel globally. In the US, drops\\nhave been observed in flight trips (both international and domestic) and other\\npublic modes, as well as international passenger vehicle trips, but domestic\\npassenger vehicle trips are recovering, indicating greater long-distance travel,\\nwhich is more likely for recreation purpose. At the same time, the use of bikes has\\nincreased, leading to more shorter trips in active modes.\\n\\n1.3.2. Travel Trend Predictions\\nSurveys have been conducted to understand travel behavior before, during, and\\nafter the pandemic. The “COVID-19 and the Future Survey” (covidfuture.org) is a\\njoint project of Arizona State University and the University of Illinois at Chicago\\nwith support from the National Science Foundation. Researchers in the project\\nteam focus on identifying the impacts that are likely to endure after the pandemic\\nis over. The survey consists of questions in different categories for “before and\\nnow and future” scenarios of COVID-19, in terms of employment,  working and\\nstudying,  shopping and dining,  daily transport,  attitudes,  demographics, and social\\nnetworks.  States  with denser populations yielded more responses (about 20\\nmetropolitan areas across the US), and Arizona is oversampled. The results are\\nweighted to match the regional and national population, in terms of age, gender,\\neducation, Hispanic population, vehicle, income, and children.\\n\\nBy mid-November, the survey showed that 20% of respondents had  been tested,\\nwith 1.6% positive, and 12% believed  that they had had COVID-19. Among all\\nrespondents, 33% had faced a decreased income, but a few people observed an\\nincrease in income. COVID-19 also caused more home relocation;  14% of\\nrespondents had moved in the seven months since April 2020, matching the\\nannual percentage of home moves in the US in all of 2019.\\n\\n23\\n\\n[PDF link](http:covidfuture.org)\\n\\n## [PDF page 39]\\n\\nSurvey results revealed trends related to travel, such as working from home, e-\\nshopping, people’s attitudes toward travel, and mode choice. An estimated 35% of\\nrespondents experienced increased productivity at home, mostly by recapturing\\ntime previously spent commuting, followed by other reasons like flexible hours\\nand comfortable spaces at home. Based on the survey results, working at home\\nwould reduce transit use by half as well as driving. This has already been\\nobserved in many cities like New York and Washington, D.C., which feature\\nreliable mass public transportation systems (Sadik-Khan and Solomonow, 2020).\\nIn terms of e-shopping, about 20% of respondents use online grocery shopping at\\nleast once per week. And among those who plan to use online grocery shopping a\\nfew times per month after the pandemic, 12.6% never used e-shopping before the\\npandemic. Most respondents agree that one should stay at home until COVID-19\\nsubsides, and they perceive high risk in the use of public transportation and\\nairplanes.  This indicates that  concerns regarding sharing space with other people\\nare the main reason for not using air travel post-pandemic, but some respondents\\nindicated that they would make more trips because they have been pent up at\\nhome for too long and desire to make up for travel that was  canceled.  Survey\\nresults also indicated that the new familiarity with conducting business meetings\\nonline would be the top reason for reduced business air trips in the future. As the\\npandemic influenced  future transportation patterns, it will impact the way AVs\\ntransform future mobility. Survey results indicate that some people will tend to\\nkeep telecommuting after the pandemic (Mokhtarian and Grossman, 2020). It will\\nbe interesting to see how the increase in teleworking and the implementation of\\nAVs would alter the way people make long-distance trips.\\n\\n24\\n\\n## [PDF page 40]\\n\\nChapter 2. Survey Design and Application\\n\\nAVs and SAVs will become increasingly available over the coming years. For\\nthis reason, the implications of these services on travel, trade, emissions, travel\\ncost, and other factors need to be anticipated across Texas. This chapter addresses\\nthe design of a long-distance passenger-travel survey to predict impacts on mode\\nand destination choices, travel preferences, VMT changes, and near-  and long-\\nterm policies and cost scenarios across emerging technologies. The survey\\nquestions as well as the analyses of responses will be explained in more detail in\\nthe next chapters.\\n\\n2.1. The survey includes a mix of\\nrevealed and stated preference questions for current or recent trips and futuristic\\nscenarios. A set of adaptative questions is included to evaluate travel time\\nchanges and users’ willingness to pay to ride in AVs. Questions related to the\\neffects  of COVID-19 are also included, and different scenarios are tested for a\\nfuture COVID-19-like virus to understand the impacts of possible future\\npandemics. Survey Data Analysis\\n\\nThe influencing factors impacting long-distance trips;  predictions of the impacts\\nof AVs, SAVs, and ATrucks on long-distance trip-making;  and impacts on\\ntourism and overall travel behavior were explored through a thorough review of\\nliterature, data, and survey responses in Chapter 1. These facets of travel behavior\\nare incredibly important in predicting network use, travel demand, and industry\\ncosts and expenses by mode and will be highly impacted by the introduction of\\nautomation technology. The most critical observations from the intensive\\nliterature review involve accepted patterns in long-distance travel in both the US\\nand Texas. Long-distance travel is heavily impacted by frequency, distance,\\nmode, destination, household income, traveler age, education level, and presence\\nof children in the household;  the opportunity for employee reimbursement is a\\nfactor in the case of long-distance travel for business.\\n\\nAutomation will allow for large cost savings as drivers will be able to spend their\\n“driving” time in more productive ways, which will lead to an altered value of\\ntravel time and higher willingness to pay for an automated mode that allows for\\nthis heightened utility. The survey conducted during this project allows\\nexamination of how AV travelers may use their time on the road and how their\\ntravel choices may impact other modes of travel. The literature review found that\\nthe most common purpose for long-distance trips is visiting friends and relatives\\nand that long-distance tourists are more likely to have higher numbers of\\ndestinations and trip purposes, greater expenditures, and trips of longer durations.\\nIt is also observed in both Texas and across the US that the primary mode for\\nlong-distance travel up to 400 miles is an automobile; beyond that distance air\\ntravel becomes the dominant mode. The survey addressed how the introduction of\\nAVs impacts this distinction in mode choice. Finally, the literature surrounding\\nthe impacts of COVID-19 indicated that air travel greatly decreased during the\\nheight of the pandemic but has since returned to near-normal levels, with the\\nnumber of longer work trips not bouncing back as quickly as the number of\\nshorter trips and an overall heightened concern about using shared modes of\\ntransportation. The survey aims to address the discussed topics in-depth and\\nprovide respondents with various options on how they would address long-\\ndistance travel with the introduction of AVs and in a post-pandemic world.\\n\\nAs referenced in-depth in previous section, the survey developed is one of the first\\nof its kind that focuses directly on long-distance travel with the use of AVs. The\\nsurvey also accrues data on multiple variables that are excluded from other\\nsurveys and data sources on this topic, such as costs of accommodation, airlines’\\nbusiness expenses, and fuel, as well as stops and total trip duration—factors that\\n\\n30\\n\\n## [PDF page 46]\\n\\ncannot be captured in typical 24-hour travel behavior surveys. The survey also\\ncontributes to new research focusing on how long-distance travel has been\\nimpacted by the COVID-19 pandemic and how the pandemic may impact\\npeople’s travel choices in the long term.\\n\\n3.1. Limitations\\nThe survey has demonstrated many useful and interesting results that help\\nanticipate Americans’ and Texans’ long-distance travel choices. However, some\\nlimitations exist in the survey design and data collection process.\\n\\nThe survey respondent pool of 1,004 represents a small sample of both Texas and\\nUS residents and has been scaled proportionally to represent the entire state and\\ncountry. These responses may include outliers despite all efforts to be as\\nrepresentative as possible of the population. More samples can help reduce the\\nsample bias, which also means a higher cost for the data collection.\\n\\nDue to the total time constraint on the survey questionnaire, only approximately\\n70 questions were asked.  Considering the multiple topics involved, including\\nautomated technology, the COVID-19 pandemic, and long-distance travel,\\n\\n50\\n\\n## [PDF page 66]\\n\\nadditional questions would help the team discover more in-depth results but\\nwould also increase the burden for respondents and thus produce an undesirable\\nresponse quality.\\n\\nThe limited time to collect data also prevented the team from collecting survey\\nresponses that perfectly match the US and Texas demographics. Assembly of  Other Datasets\\n\\nAssembly of datasets is a vital step in creating a long-distance travel demand\\nmodel that leverages this project’s survey model. Because the LD-AV survey\\nrepresents a subsample of the entire population, it is necessary to use other\\nresources to properly model the entire population. After the data sources and\\nmodels are identified, and their scales and caveats are understood, it is also\\nnecessary to consider how to combine different data sources using scientific,\\nrepeatable processes. Here, models using these components will be finalized,\\nincluding identifying parameters for those models that will be true to the\\nsubsamples found in this and other projects’ surveys on long-distance travel,\\nvehicle ownership, and AV usage.\\n\\nThis section is organized to first introduce the model structure, followed by\\nfurther explorations of each major dataset that feeds into it. This document then\\ntouches on prior work around models that predict AV ownership and usage, an\\nimportant aspect that is also challenging to predict. Finally, a separate exploration\\nis made into freight models to support the creation of an AV long-distance freight\\nmodel.\\n\\n4.1. Model  Structure\\nThe modeling framework of this study begins with a population generation stage,\\nfeeding into travel choice and then destination and mode choice. The final\\noutcome is a set of disaggregate long-distance trips that represent all long-\\ndistance travel of a future US population that lives with a market where AVs are\\nreadily available as a viable mode choice. A separate freight module produces\\ndisaggregate long-distance freight trips.\\n\\nWhile the Texas Department of Transportation (TxDOT) focuses on long-distance\\ntravel among Texans, the researchers found it important to model long-distance\\ntravel for the entire US due to the pervasive interconnections between their travel\\nnetworks. This is because of the significant number of trips where Texans travel\\noutside of the state, visitors come to Texas, and non-Texans pass through Texas.\\nThis also provides opportunities to contrast Texans’ travel patterns with those of\\nthe rest of the US. When the nationwide model is completed, it will be\\nstraightforward to analyze results that affect Texas with an anticipated higher\\ndegree of accuracy.\\n\\nA microsimulation model requires a representation of the full population of\\ninterest (i.e., the population of the United States). The PopGen synthesizer was\\n\\n52\\n\\n## [PDF page 68]\\n\\nused to generate a synthetic population. ACS Public Use Micro Sample (PUMS)\\ndata will be used as the population seed. Individuals within the synthesized\\npopulation will be allocated according to the rJourney National Use Microdata\\nArea (NUMA) travel analysis zone system, allowing us to adopt rJourney data\\nand validate spatial patterns against their results. (Further detail about rJourney\\nand its NUMA zone system is found later in this chapter).\\n\\nThe next stage of the model will represent a set of “pre-trip” decisions by\\nhouseholds. Such processes include the decision to participate in long-distance\\ntravel, tour frequency over the course of a year, and party size for each tour.\\nResults from the recently completed long-distance AV (LD-AV)  survey by the\\nproject team will be combined with NHTS and regional long-distance travel data\\nto estimate and validate these models.\\n\\nThe final stage of the model comprises destination and mode choice for each\\nlong-distance tour. The mode choice will be conditional upon a household AV\\nownership choice model. An existing AV ownership model for the US developed\\nby the project team in 2017 will be updated for this purpose. A 2021 survey of\\nAmericans’ preferences for AVs will be used to adjust the model, as it asked a\\nparallel set of questions to the 2017 study. Mode and destination choice models\\nwill use a variety of data sources to generate alternative attributes for model\\nestimation. The DB1B database from the Bureau of Transportation Statistics\\n(BTS) provides both a source for air travel attributes (e.g., fare, travel time, and\\nnumber of legs) and a validation of total annual travel through expansion of its\\n10% sample. Other datasets include Amtrak route details and NHTS long-distance\\ntrip records.\\n\\n4.2. (2017) modeled individual preferences for ownership and sharing of\\nAVs using education, age, income, employment status, household composition,\\nand experience of ride sharing and car crashing. The results showed that 15.4% of\\nrespondents were interested in AV ownership and sharing. A  study conducted by\\nZhang et al. (2018) modeled vehicle ownership reduction and unoccupied VMT\\nbased on the advent of AVs using travel surveys and synthesized trip profiles\\nfrom the Atlanta metropolitan area. The study developed a greedy algorithm,\\nwhich showed that more than 18%  of households can reduce vehicle ownership\\nwhile maintaining their current travel patterns; that is equivalent to a 9.5%\\nreduction in private vehicles in the study region. The study found that if travelers’\\nschedules are relaxed by 15 minutes, up to 24.1%  of households are likely to\\neliminate at least one of their current private vehicles. The study also applied a\\nlogistic regression model, which showed that people who live in suburban areas\\nand have high income levels are more likely to reduce vehicle ownership as AVs\\n\\n65\\n\\n## [PDF page 81]\\n\\nbecome available. A more recent study by Lee et al. (2019) assessed factors that\\ninfluence people’s intentions to use AVs. The demographic factors used in the\\nstudy include age, gender, marital status, monthly income, and current vehicle\\nownership. A structural equation model was estimated in this study to examine\\nrelationships between perceived usefulness, intention to use, perceived risks, and\\nease of use.\\n\\nIn  another study by Kim et al. (2020), 3,106 respondents in Georgia were asked\\nabout short-term impacts of AVs on mode choice, medium-term impacts on\\nactivity patterns, and long-term impacts on behavior change. They used a cross-\\nnested logit model for modeling the choice of home location and vehicle\\nownership. The results indicated that those with more vehicles than the number of\\nhousehold members of driving age are more likely to let go of vehicles. The\\nyounger pro-suburban individuals were more likely to move farther away from\\ntheir current location after adopting an AV.\\n\\nFurthermore, Bansal and Kockelman (2016) put forward a simulation-based fleet\\nevolution network to forecast long-term adoption of connected and autonomous\\ntechnologies by Americans. Respondents were asked about their preferences\\ntowards their household’s annual vehicle transactions and CAV technologies.\\nSimilar activity pattern changes were studied by Le-Klähn et al. (2019), using\\nSimMobility (an integrated simulation model) to assess how AV services change\\nrespondents’ preferences and attitudes. This study also tried to determine changes\\nin house location and vehicle ownership.\\n\\nIn addition to AV ownership models, a study conducted by Maeng and Cho\\n(2022) aimed to assess consumer choice and usage patterns in anticipation of\\nSAVs’ upcoming launch into the market. Silva et al.\\n(2021) used  a case study conducted in Budapest, Hungary, to analyze the impacts\\nof AV acceptability and usage of shared vehicles on parking demand. They used\\nthe responses collected in the survey to build present, transitional, and future\\nscenarios to quantify the gradual changes in AV ownership. Trip Frequency\\nThe long-distance trip frequency model was developed using the zero-inflated\\nnegative binomial distribution based on population-weighted 2016/17 NHTS trip\\ndata for domestic travels. A zero-inflated model assumes that a “zero outcome”\\ncomes from two different processes. In this case, it starts with a decision process\\nabout whether or not a person is making a long-distance trip (>75 miles). If the\\nperson decides not to make a long-distance trip, the only possible outcome is zero.\\nIf the person is making a long-distance trip, then a count model is utilized to\\npredict how many trips will be made.\\n\\nThe two parts of the zero-inflated negative binomial model are, first, a logit model\\nto decide whether a person will  make a long-distance trip or not, and second, a\\nnegative binomial count model to find the number of trips. Trip-  Chaining  in NHTS Sample\\nThe aforementioned model outcomes are applicable to individual trip links\\nexceeding 75 miles from the NHTS trip file. In the course of this investigation, we\\nhave treated each trip segment from the NHTS trip file as an individual trip,\\nincluding those segments that entail brief stops en-route to the primary\\ndestination. For example, a 150-mile trip from Austin to Houston that involves a\\nrefueling stop shows as two separate trips (one for “shopping” midway, and one\\nfor the true purpose of the trip at the final destination). Long-distance (LD) trips\\nare defined as those with the real destination (not an en route “pit stop” for gas or\\nfood) more than 75-miles away (on the travel network). To address the limitation\\nin segments vs true trips, we developed an algorithm to identify intermediate\\n“trips” that are really just pit stops in a longer-distance trip-chain en route to a\\nfinal destination (resulting in fewer true LD trips). The algorithm is also designed\\nto fuse “short” (less than 75-mile one-way) trip segments into long-distance (LD)\\ntrips (more than 75-miles one-way) as well as “long” (>75 miles) and “short”\\n(<75 miles) trip segments with each when they can be considered part of chain to\\nthe final destination. Thus, the number of LD trips may rise or fall, relative to a\\nsimple counting of segments that are 75-miles or longer (which is the technique\\nthat most analysts use). The algorithm reflects trip coordinates (to appreciate trip\\ndirection, thereby avoiding back and forth trips or tours to many true destinations\\n[like delivery chains]), dwell times at “destinations” (at the end of every trip\\nsegment, to avoid counting relatively short “pitstops”), and trip purpose (to\\ndistinguish refueling and meals en route, for example, from a longer-duration\\nfinal-destination activity).\\n\\nAfter applying the algorithm’s many rules, the NHTS 2016/17 sample’s LD trips\\n(i.e., those more than 75 miles one-way) fell by just 3.4% (from 1.84 one-way LD\\ntrips per American per month to 1.78). This brings the total number of NHTS\\nperson-trips down by 0.88%, with the average American making 3.47 trips per\\nday instead of the previously estimated 3.50 trips. Notably, the algorithm was\\nonly applied to trips or chains of trips that met the criteria for long-distance travel\\n(those segments more than 75 miles each or a series of related segments adding to\\nmore than 75 miles one-way), ensuring that it did not impact shorter trips.\\n\\nThe best predictor in distinguishing pit stops are the coordinates (lat and long) of\\nstopping points Successive trip segments by each NHTS respondent were used to\\ndiscern whether distance from the origin kept rising in a directed way, or started\\npivoting (or even falling), indicating changes in direction. If the Euclidean\\ndistance from the chain origin started falling (after rising after earlier stops), it\\nindicated a return trip. Combined with other factors (including mode changes, site\\nactivity/trip-end purpose, and short-activity durations), these falling distances or\\nchanges in direction helped distinguish trip chains. Mode shifts (like driving to or\\ntaking a bus to an airport, and changing planes at a hub airport) are not real\\ndestinations. Additionally, stopping away from the origin during a long-distance\\ntrip, to purchase food or gasoline, is often not a true destination -  especially when\\nthe stop is short and trip direction unchanged.\\n\\n99\\n\\n## [PDF page 115]\\n\\nMeal and carry-out stops shorter than 90 minutes and general errand stops (like to\\na post office) shorter than 15 minutes are assumed to be part of a longer trip.\\nWhile the algorithm is designed to identify and classify long-distance trips more\\naccurately, there are limitations to pitstop inference. For example, it is challenging\\nto determine whether a person stopped to purchase gas or a breakfast coffee when\\nsetting out on a long-distance trip.  The NHTS “WHYTO” purpose categories\\n(shown above) do not distinguish fuel stops from grocery or clothing-shop stops,\\nand do not distinguish errand types (like a visit to the post office versus a library),\\nmaking it difficult to categorize these as true destinations or pit stops along the\\nway. To address this challenge, a destination dwell time threshold of 30 minutes\\n(for fuel/shopping) and 15 minutes (for errands) is assumed to help identify longer\\nstops that may indicate a true purpose. Some of these stops should be considered\\nas necessary, separate, or true destinations that would have been made regardless\\nof the longer trip that day. Similarly, stops near the end of a long-distance trip\\nmay be trips that would have been made anyway upon arrival at the destination.\\nTravelers have many options in how they chain trips, and some important\\ndestinations may be along one’s long-distance trip route.\\n\\nWhen “pit stops\'\' (short stops, typically to eat, refuel, change modes, etc.) on\\nlong-distance trips are no longer counted as destinations (thanks to the\\nalgorithm’s application), only the attributes of the final leg of a trip chain\\n(variables of travel day trip purpose [WHYTRP90] and trip purpose summary\\n[WHYTRP1S]) are used to determine the LD trip purpose. This approach reduces\\nthe shares of LD trips taken for commutes plus work trips, shopping, meals/food,\\nand other volunteer activities/change in mode (indicated by the “97= Something\\nelse” purpose) by 10.8, 35.5, 74.2, and 54.9 percentage points, respectively.\\nRemoving such pit stops raises the shares of (1) school plus religious trips, (2)\\nmedical trips, (3) transporting someone, and (4) social trips (visiting friends and\\nrelatives) plus recreational trips, by 14.8, 16.7, 20.8 and 21.0 percentage points,\\nrespectively. Average and median LD person-trip lengths also rise (after applying\\nthe algorithm), by about 10 percent: from 268.5 to 289.9 (average LD trip) miles\\nand from 129.2 to 138.5 (median) miles, respectively.  This algorithm considers\\nthe location, timing, and sequence features of sample “trips” to infer the real\\nreasons behind long-distance travels (where many “long” [> 75-mile] and/or\\n“short” [< 75-mile] segments may be describing a single long-distance trip).\\nOverall, this algorithm provides a more accurate and comprehensive\\nunderstanding of true long-distance travel patterns, accounting for the complex\\nnature of multi-stop trips and ensuring that the resulting data is meaningful for\\ntransportation planning and policy. This discrepancy has the potential to alter the\\noutcomes of trip frequency and trip purpose models. Nevertheless, we anticipate\\nthat the increase on long-distance trips is approximately 10%.\\n\\n100\\n\\n## [PDF page 116]\\n\\nTable  36  . Freight  Model Specification\\n\\nThe implementation of autonomous trucking will bring sweeping changes to the\\nworld of freight transport. Semi-automated trucks may enable automated driving\\nunder supervision and limited circumstances, such as driving long distances on an\\ninterstate highway. Eventually, fully automated self-driving trucks (or ATrucks)\\nmay leave the truck terminal and travel to a destination without human\\nintervention or presence in the truck cab (Viscelli, 2018). ATrucks may be able to\\nautomate other functions in addition to onboard tasks like drop-offs and pickups,\\nbut most experts expect an attendant will remain on board, doing other types of\\nwork, sleeping as needed, and ensuring thoughtful deliveries and pickups\\n(Yankelevich, et al., 2018). Such multi-tasking of vehicle attendants will allow for\\nextended use of commercial trucks (i.e., every day, almost 24 hours a day) and\\ngreater labor productivity, resulting in lower per-mile and per-ton-mile freight\\ndelivery costs.\\n\\nIn 2014, trucks carried 1.996 trillion ton-miles of freight around the US, 37.7% of\\nthe nation’s total ton-miles transported that year (BTS, 2017). Investment in and\\nuse of ATrucks will affect not only national and regional economies (Clements\\nand Kockelman, 2017) but trade patterns, production levels, and goods pricing.\\nCommercial trucks consume about 20% of the nation’s transportation fuel, and\\nself-driving technologies are predicted to reduce those diesel fuel bills by 4–7%\\n101\\n\\n## [PDF page 117]\\n\\n(Liu and Kockelman, 2017; Barth et al., 2004; Shladover et al., 2006). ATrucks\\ncan reduce some environmental impacts, lower crash rates, and increase line-haul\\ntransportation. Platooned convoys should enable following truck attendants to\\navoid certain restrictions on service hours, enabling longer driving distances.\\nUranga (2017) predicts greater use of ATrucks before passenger vehicle\\nautomation, thanks to the more obvious economic benefits of self-driving trucks.\\n\\nWhile there is active investigative interest in the travel and traffic effects of self-\\ndriving cars, research into the travel and traffic impacts of ATrucks is dearly\\nlacking. This project leverages Freight Analysis Framework 5 (FAF5) to estimate\\nthe mode and origin choices of freight carriers;  then, model parameters are fed\\ninto the random-utility-based multi-regional input-output (RUBMRIO) model to\\ninvestigate how patterns of freight flow will change based on automation\\ntechnology’s impacts on truck cost and operation. ATrucks’ per-mile operating\\ncost is assumed to be 50% of that of HTrucks’, factoring in the benefits of\\nincreased safety, a lower wage for truck drivers, and a higher initial cost (e.g.,\\npurchase of tractor) to introduce ATrucks.\\n\\nThe remainder of this chapter proceeds through each component of the freight\\nmodels, showing how it is estimated and parameterized and offering insight into\\nsignificant trends that will affect the overall RUBMRIO model.\\n\\n6.1. Feedback loops are performed to\\nprovide consistent results between travel time and cost skims and network\\nassignment flows, feeding congested travel times back for subsequent iterations,\\nusing the method of successive averages.\\n\\nA multi-modal, multi-class assignment was conducted in each scenario to reflect\\nlarge differences in VOTT between human drivers and self-driving vehicles. The\\nfeedback loop was set to perform 20 iterations, with a stopping criterion of a\\nrelative gap below 10-4, to try and achieve a stable, convergent equilibrium.\\n\\n7.6. Conclusions\\nThis report applies long-distance travel demand models for passengers and freight\\nacross the US and Texas, with and without the inclusion of AVs and ATrucks,\\nwhich are expected on Texas roadways in the upcoming decades. We\\nmicrosimulate long-distance (over 75 miles one-way) travel choices and vehicle\\nownership choices for a 10% sample of the US population, and for freight\\nsimulations, we use TxDOT’s SAM-V4 as a four-step, traditional application.\\nBoth applications are for domestic travel only. The passenger travel model\\nindicated that in 2019, there were expected to be 0.85 vehicles per capita in the\\nUS, which is consistent with the estimate of 0.83 vehicles per capita in 2020\\nbased on US census data. AV ownership per capita is likely to be 0.33 vehicles\\nafter their introduction, assuming a $3,500 technology premium in 2040. Two\\nlong-distance trips per month per capita were estimated for the 10% synthetic\\npopulation, which matches the NHTS data. Mode splits for long-distance,\\ndomestic trips prior to AV access were estimated as 64.10% by private\\nautomobile, 30.42% by rental car, and 5.49% by airplane. After AVs become\\navailable at $0.70 per mile operation cost, mode splits shift to 31.67% by\\nconventional HV, 23.02% by conventional rental car, 23.54% by AV, 18.24% by\\nSAVs, and  3.53% by air. Assuming a $3,500 technology cost premium (e.g., in\\nyear 2040), total PMT  per capita in long-distance trips is estimated to raise 35%,\\nfrom 280 to 379 per month.\\n\\nIn the short term, assuming that ATrucks cost 1.5 times as much as HTrucks but\\nsave the latter’s dwelling time, 1.7 trillion tons of goods are anticipated to be\\ntransported by HTrucks and ATrucks across Texas in 2045, while the remaining\\ngoods will be transported by CL (23.5%) and IM (16.5%). All 15 modeled\\nindustries would witness increases in truck trips and decreases in CL and IM trips\\ndue to the use of ATrucks. Across all commodities transported in tons, ton-miles\\ntransported by trucks will increase 7.8%, while ton-miles transported by CL and\\nIM will  drop by 12.6% and 2.3%, respectively. In the long term, ATruck cost may\\ndrop below HTruck cost when on-board truck drivers are no longer required.\\nWhen ATruck cost drops to half of HTruck cost, truck mode share increases by\\n4.2% and the number of tons transported by truck increases an additional 7.3%.\\nSuch cost decreases will also bring an over 10% increase in trucks’ mode share\\nfor transporting certain commodities like food, paper, and primary metal. They\\nmay also lead to an over 60% increase in truck mode choice for a few selected\\ncommodities that do not have a high share of truck use to start with, but this does\\nnot significantly impact the truck mode share.\\n\\n132\\n\\n## [PDF page 148]\\n\\nChapter 8. Value  of  Research  (VoR):  LD-AV\\n\\nQuantitative valuation of research projects is difficult since agency implementation\\nof the research results is not yet known. Two assessment areas, value of travel time\\nsavings  and  safety  benefits,  are  examined  here  to  arrive  at  benefit-cost  ratios\\n(BCRs)  for  TxDOT  Research  and  Technology  Innovation  Project  0-7081,\\n“Understanding  the  Impact  of  Autonomous  Vehicles  on  Long-Distance  Travel\\nMode and Destination Choice in Texas.” The project delivers model equations and\\nparameters, as well as direct estimates of AVs’ impacts on long-distance passenger\\nand  freight  travel  in  Texas.  If  these  models  and  estimates  are  used  in  TxDOT’s\\ntransportation planning process and those of regional MPOs, border towns, freight\\ncarriers, airlines, and ports, Texans can expect a more efficient, less congested, and\\nhigher-welfare  future.  This  is  because  this  project’s  results  will  help  planners,\\nengineers,  and  businesses  prepare  for  a  future  with  AVs—including  SAVs  and\\nATrucks. In addition to the benefits quantified here of lowered driving burdens for\\nAV  travelers  and  benefits  of  improved  infrastructure  that  supports  long-distance\\nAV  journeys,  the  project  has  other  quantifiable  benefits.  Examples  include  the\\nfollowing:\\n\\n•  better understanding of future travel demand that can help inform\\nappropriate roadway user fees that are fair and supportive of infrastructure\\nmaintenance (to complement motor fuel taxes) for freight and passenger\\ntravel in smart vehicles.\\n\\n•  economic benefits (like lower-cost shipping, retail development that caters\\nto more roadway users, and avoidance of overbuilt parking lots and\\nunnecessary airport expansions) from anticipating, designing for, and\\nessentially welcoming AVs onto Texas roadways; and\\n\\n•  better planning for added pavement maintenance needs, which will result\\nfrom higher roadway use rates, thanks to AVs making “driving” easier.\\n\\nPerceived Travel  Time  Benefits  (via Lower  Driving Burdens)\\n\\nBy  facilitating  planning  for  and  responding  to  AV  use  of  Texas  roadways,  this\\nproject  ultimately  enables  lower-cost  travel.  It  does  so  in  two  ways:  (1)  reducing\\nthe  perceived  burden  of  travel  for  those  previously  driving  cars  and  trucks  by\\nenabling an infrastructure that supports better use of travelers’ time, and (2) opening\\nup new modes of travel so that many travelers and some goods avoid the costs and\\nchallenges of air travel or rail use by staying on the roadways.\\n\\n133\\n\\n## [PDF page 149]\\n\\nVarious  assumptions  are  used  to  perform  this  assessment. All  monetary  values  are\\nexpressed  in  year  2022  dollars,  unless  otherwise  noted.  Although  travel  demand\\nand congestion are expected to rise over time, this analysis relies on network traffic\\nlevels from 2019, to avoid COVID-19 impacts.\\n\\nAnnual congestion costs:  Roadway delay costs were estimated to be as follows in\\nTexas’s major regions (Schrank et al., 2021):\\n\\nDelay  Cost  Hours Wasted\\nMetro Area  (2019, in (2019, in millions)\\nbillions)\\nHouston  $5.66  263\\nDallas-Fort  Worth  $4.81  220\\nAustin  $1.73  81.1\\nSan Antonio  $1.58  71.9\\nTOTAL  $13.8  636\\n\\nValue of travel time (VOTT):  Without AVs, the value of travel time for commuter\\ndrivers is estimated to be $20 per hour (Schrank et al., 2021). (2020)  and  others  have\\nestimated  that  “driver”  VOTT  will  fall  by  about  32%  and  24%  in  suburban  and\\nurban  settings,  respectively.  (“Non-driving”  passengers’  VOTT  is  assumed  not  to\\nchange).  Using  the  midpoint  of  these  percentages,  28%,  drivers’  VOTT  while\\nriding in an AV (along with those of passengers) is likely to average around $14.52\\nper hour (pivoting off of Schrank et al.’s 2021 estimate).\\n\\nLong-distance  AV  mode  share  on  roadways:  Assuming  a  readily  available\\nsupply  of  AVs  in  the  marketplace,  this  research  project  forecasts  that  for  long-\\ndistance  passenger  travel  in  Texas,  conventional  passenger  vehicles  will  have  a\\nmode  share  of  just  31.67%  in  2040,  down  from  64.10%  today,  with  AVs  making\\nup  a  41%  share.  (Air  travel  and  rental  vehicles  account  for  the  remaining).  This\\nmeans that roughly 43% (41/(41  + 32+ 23) = 0.33) of ground travelers will be using\\nAVs for their long-distance travels by 2040.\\n\\nCongestion  cost  savings:  The  difference  in  congestion  costs  in  2040  between  a\\nscenario with AVs and a business-as-usual scenario without AVs can be computed\\nas follows:\\n\\n\ud835G  =  \ud835/  +  ℎ(\ud835G  −  \ud835/)(1  −  \ud835)\\n\\nwhere:\\nc0  = Total cost of congestion prior to AV introduction\\nc1  = Total cost of congestion in 2040, after AV introduction\\nh  = Number of hours wasted due to congestion (using today’s congestion\\nas a proxy)\\n\\n134\\n\\n## [PDF page 150]\\n\\nv0  = VOTT for those in conventional vehicles\\nv1  = VOTT for those riding in AVs\\nm = Mode share predicted for personal commuter transport in 2040\\n\\nThe  total  congestion  cost  in  the  scenario  with  AVs  is  $11.4  billion  in  2040,  with  a\\nperceived  savings  of  $2.41 billion per  year  (assuming  2019  traffic  volumes  persist\\nyear after year, which is conservative).\\n\\nContribution share of this research: While the researchers believe that the work\\nperformed in this project is important for TxDOT to successfully integrate AVs into\\ntheir long-distance travel demand forecasting by 2040, they acknowledge that many\\nefforts funded by TxDOT will contribute to this. Gravity models in their traditional form consist of\\nproduction, attraction (e.g., tourism attractions, population, and language of the\\ndestination), friction (i.e., travel time and/or fare), and a gravity constant term. A\\nlogarithmic operator was applied to form a log-linear gravity model, and an\\nordinary-least-squares (OLS) model was estimated to find the number of trips\\ndistributed between each origin and destination pair. Friction factor here is a\\nfunction of impedance incorporating auto and air travel times and cost (i.e., flight\\nfare, highway toll) normalized by value of time (VOT). VOT is assumed to be\\n$30 per hour for air travelers and $20 per hour for auto users. Table 52 shows the\\nspecifications of this log-linear model as well as the practical significance of\\ndifferent statistically significant variables. This model was estimated using data\\nfrom multiple sources indicating trip production for 334 major US airports and\\ncountry attractions for 1,028 international airports in countries other than the US.\\nThere is a lack of data for origins and destinations of land travelers to Canada and\\nMexico. For the former, major airports in most touristic cities  in Canadian\\nprovinces that are accessible from the US (e.g., Ontario, Quebec, British\\nColumbia, Alberta, Nova Scotia) are considered as the destination locations.\\nOrigins are assumed to be the major airport of the closest state in the US. For\\nMexico, all trips are aggregated in one origin and destination pair from Texas to\\nthe state of Sinaloa. The trip distribution model indicated that trips to a foreign\\ndestination from an American origin fall 41% when the travel time increases by 7\\nhours or plane ticket cost rises by $210. Destinations hosting tourist attractions\\nincrease OD flow by 48%. The population and English-speaking indicators of the\\ndestination country are neither practically nor statistically significant.\\n\\n236\\n\\n## [PDF page 252]\\n\\nTable  52.
